why: GRC teams hire people who can talk to IT, to the business and to auditors in the same week. Before any framework, recruiters check that you understand what governance, risk and compliance each mean, how a security control works, who owns what, and how one control answers several laws and standards at once.
outcome: explain governance, risk and compliance and the three lines model, describe assets, threats and vulnerabilities with the CIA triad, classify and test controls, map one control to ISO 27001, NIST CSF, GDPR and NIS2, structure a policy set, run an access review and report key risk indicators to management.

lessons.title: What GRC is and who does what
text: GRC stands for governance, risk and compliance. Governance is how an organisation sets direction and makes decisions about information security: who decides, which rules apply, how much risk is acceptable, and how management stays informed. Risk management is the method for finding what could go wrong, measuring it and deciding what to do about it. Compliance is proving that the organisation meets its obligations: laws such as GDPR or NIS2, standards such as ISO 27001, and commitments made to clients in contracts.

The three are linked. Governance writes the rules and the risk appetite, risk management tells you where the rules matter most, and compliance checks that the rules are applied and produces the evidence. A GRC analyst works across all three: keeping the risk register up to date, mapping controls to requirements, collecting evidence for audits, following action plans, reviewing suppliers and writing or updating policies.

Most organisations organise control with the three lines model. The first line is the business and IT teams that own the risks and run the controls every day: the IT team that grants access, the HR team that runs onboarding. The second line sets the framework and challenges the first line: the CISO (RSSI in France), the risk and compliance teams, the data protection officer. The third line is internal audit, which gives management and the board an independent view. Many GRC analysts sit in the second line.

Typical titles are GRC analyst, IT risk analyst, compliance analyst, information security officer and, in consulting, GRC consultant. The job is less technical than a security engineer’s, but you must understand the technology well enough to know whether a control really works. You will spend a lot of time in meetings and documents, and your value comes from clear writing, method and follow-up.

A useful habit from day one: every statement you make should be traceable. A risk has an owner and a date, a control has an owner and evidence, a decision has a name and a record. Auditors and regulators do not accept “we usually do it”: they ask to see it.
points: Governance: direction, roles, rules and risk appetite, decided by management.
Risk management: identify, assess, treat and monitor what could go wrong.
Compliance: meet laws, standards and contracts, and prove it with evidence.
Three lines: first line owns and runs controls, second line frames and challenges, third line (internal audit) gives independent assurance.
Everything traceable: an owner, a date and evidence for every risk, control and decision.

example.code:
A week of a GRC analyst
Mon  Update the risk register with IT after a new cloud project
Tue  Collect evidence for the ISO 27001 surveillance audit (access reviews, backups)
Wed  Review a new SaaS supplier: security questionnaire and contract clauses
Thu  Follow up the action plan from last year's audit findings (7 open, 2 late)
Fri  Prepare the monthly risk dashboard for the security committee
example.note: Each task touches governance (committee, policies), risk (register, supplier) and compliance (audit, evidence).

lessons.title: Information security basics: assets, threats and the CIA triad
text: Information security protects three properties of information, the CIA triad. Confidentiality: only authorised people can read it (customer files, salaries, source code). Integrity: it is accurate and only changed by authorised people and processes (bank details, prices, medical records). Availability: it can be used when needed (the online shop on Black Friday, the hospital system at night). For each asset, one property usually matters more than the others, and that drives the controls.

An asset is anything of value to the organisation: information (the customer database), the systems that process it (servers, laptops, SaaS tools), people with know-how, sites and suppliers. Asset inventories are the starting point of every risk assessment and of ISO 27001: you cannot protect what you do not know you have. Each asset needs an owner, usually a business manager, not the IT team.

A threat is something that could cause harm: a criminal group sending phishing e-mails, ransomware, an employee making a mistake, a fire, a supplier going bankrupt. A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use: an unpatched server, a shared password, no backup, a single supplier. A risk exists when a threat can exploit a vulnerability on an asset with an impact. Remove the vulnerability or reduce the impact, and the risk goes down.

Common attacks every GRC analyst should be able to explain are phishing (stealing passwords or installing malware through a fake message), ransomware (encrypting data and demanding payment, often after stealing it too), business e-mail compromise (a fake supplier asking to change bank details), exploitation of unpatched internet-facing systems, and abuse of excessive access by insiders. Most of them are stopped or limited by simple controls: multi-factor authentication, patching, backups kept offline, least privilege and awareness.

Security works in layers, called defence in depth: no single control is perfect, so you combine prevention (MFA, filtering), detection (logging and alerts) and response (incident procedure, backups). When you assess a control, ask what happens if it fails and which other layer catches the problem.
points: Confidentiality, integrity, availability: decide which matters most for each asset.
Asset: information, systems, people, sites, suppliers; each with a business owner.
Threat (what could cause harm) + vulnerability (weakness) + impact on an asset = risk.
Phishing, ransomware, fake bank-detail changes, unpatched systems and insider misuse cover most incidents.
Defence in depth: prevent, detect, respond; never rely on one control.

example.code:
Asset               Owner            Most important   Example threat          Vulnerability
Customer database   Sales director   Confidentiality  Phishing, data theft    No MFA on remote access
Payroll file        HR director      Integrity        Fake bank-detail change No call-back check
Online shop         E-commerce lead  Availability     Ransomware              Backups on the same network
Laptops             IT manager       Confidentiality  Theft in transport      Disk not encrypted
example.note: An extract of an asset and threat inventory: the business owns the asset, and the most important property points to the right control.

lessons.title: Controls: types, design and evidence
text: A control is a measure that reduces a risk. Controls are classified in two ways. By purpose: preventive controls stop the event (MFA, firewall, approval before payment), detective controls find it (log monitoring, reconciliations, access reviews), corrective controls limit the damage and restore (backups, incident response, disaster recovery). By nature: organisational controls (policies, roles, supplier contracts), people controls (screening, training, disciplinary process), physical controls (badges, locked server rooms) and technological controls (encryption, patching, logging). ISO 27001 uses these last four themes.

A control can be manual or automated. Automated controls, such as a system that blocks a login without MFA, are more reliable and easier to test, because they behave the same way every time. Manual controls, such as a manager approving access requests, depend on people, so they need clear instructions, a record and a reviewer.

Auditors test two things. Design: if the control works as described, does it really reduce the risk? An access review that only checks names and never checks rights is badly designed. Operating effectiveness: was the control actually performed, every time, during the period? They take a sample, for example 25 of 300 new joiners, and look for the evidence: the ticket, the approval, the date.

Evidence is anything that proves a control ran: a dated and signed review, a system export, a screenshot of a configuration with the date, a log extract, meeting minutes. Good evidence is complete, dated, attributable to a person and kept where you can find it again. A large part of a GRC analyst’s work is making evidence easy to produce, so that audits do not become a crisis.

Controls are documented in a control matrix: an identifier, a description written so that anyone can test it, the risk it addresses, the owner, the frequency, manual or automated, the evidence expected and the requirements it covers. A well-written control says who does what, when and how it is recorded: “Each quarter, the IT manager reviews the administrator accounts of the ERP and records the review and the removals in the ticket tool.”
points: Purpose: preventive, detective, corrective.
Nature (ISO 27001 themes): organisational, people, physical, technological.
Design (would it work?) and operating effectiveness (did it run, every time?).
Good evidence is complete, dated, attributable and easy to find.
A testable control states who, what, when, how often and what record is kept.

example.code:
ID     Control                                                  Type         Owner       Frequency  Evidence
AC-01  New access granted only after the manager's approval      Preventive   IT support  Each time  Ticket with approval
AC-04  Quarterly review of ERP admin accounts, removals logged   Detective    IT manager  Quarterly  Signed review + ticket
BK-02  Daily backup of the file server, copy kept offline        Corrective   IT ops      Daily      Backup report
BK-03  Restore test of one backup                                Detective    IT ops      Quarterly  Test report
example.note: Four lines of a control matrix. A restore test proves that backups (BK-02) actually work.

lessons.title: The map of frameworks and laws
text: Frameworks are structured sets of good practices; laws and regulations are obligations. ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard for an information security management system (ISMS), the one companies get certified against; ISO 27002 explains its controls in detail. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, published in 2024, organises security outcomes in six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover; it is free, popular in the US and used everywhere as a common language. The CIS Critical Security Controls are a prioritised list of technical measures, useful for small organisations.

Other frameworks appear in job offers. SOC 2 is an American audit report on a service provider’s controls, based on the trust services criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy); a type II report covers how the controls worked over a period, usually 6 to 12 months. PCI DSS applies to anyone who stores, processes or transmits payment card data. COBIT is a framework for the governance of IT as a whole, often used by IT auditors.

The main European laws are GDPR, which protects personal data in every sector; NIS2, the directive on the cybersecurity of essential and important entities (energy, transport, health, digital infrastructure and many more), with management accountability and incident reporting; and DORA, the regulation on the digital operational resilience of the financial sector, applied since January 2025, which covers ICT risk, incidents, resilience testing and IT providers. In France, the national agency ANSSI publishes guidance and the CNIL supervises personal data.

The key skill is mapping: one well-designed control usually answers several requirements at once. Multi-factor authentication on remote access supports ISO 27001 controls on authentication, NIST CSF Protect, GDPR’s security obligation (article 32), NIS2’s risk management measures and SOC 2 criteria. GRC teams keep one control set mapped to every framework they must follow, so each control is tested once and the evidence is reused, instead of running a separate project per standard.

When you read a job offer, notice which texts it names: ISO 27001 and NIS2 point to an industrial or public organisation, SOC 2 to a software company selling to American clients, DORA to a bank, an insurer or one of their IT providers. Prepare examples for those.
points: ISO 27001: certifiable ISMS standard; ISO 27002: guidance on its controls.
NIST CSF 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
SOC 2 type II: auditor’s report on a provider’s controls over a period; PCI DSS: card data.
GDPR (personal data), NIS2 (critical and important sectors), DORA (finance, since January 2025).
Map one control set to all frameworks: test once, reuse the evidence.

example.code:
Control: MFA required for all remote access and administrator accounts
  ISO 27001:2022   Annex A 8.5 Secure authentication
  NIST CSF 2.0     PR.AA  Identity management, authentication and access control
  GDPR             Article 32 Security of processing
  NIS2             Article 21 (2)(j) multi-factor authentication
  SOC 2            CC6.1 Logical access security
example.note: One control, five requirements: a mapping like this lets one test and one piece of evidence serve every audit.

lessons.title: Policies, standards and procedures
text: Governance is written down in a hierarchy of documents. The information security policy is a short document approved by top management: objectives, scope, roles and the commitment to comply and improve. Topic policies cover one area each: access control, acceptable use, supplier security, backups, incident management, cryptography. Standards set mandatory, measurable rules (“passwords of at least 12 characters, MFA for remote access”). Procedures explain step by step how to do something. Guidelines are recommendations, not obligations.

A good policy is short, clear and applicable. It says what must be done and who is responsible, not how to configure each tool; that belongs in standards and procedures, which change more often. Write for the reader: an employee must understand the acceptable use policy in five minutes, while the IT team needs a precise technical standard.

Every document has an owner, a version, an approval date and a review date, usually once a year or after a major change such as a new law, an incident or a reorganisation. People must know the policies apply to them: they read and accept them at onboarding, and awareness campaigns remind them. An unread policy is not a control.

Exceptions are normal: a legacy system cannot support MFA, a supplier refuses an audit clause. A good governance process lets the business request an exception, assesses the risk, has the risk owner accept it for a limited time with compensating controls, and records it in an exception register reviewed regularly. Hidden exceptions are much more dangerous than recorded ones.

In France, the information security policy is often called PSSI (politique de sécurité des systèmes d’information), and public bodies follow the State’s PSSIE. In interviews, being able to describe the document set, its life cycle and how exceptions are handled shows that you have seen governance in practice, not only in theory.
points: Policy (why and what, approved by management) → standard (mandatory measurable rules) → procedure (how, step by step) → guideline (advice).
Owner, version, approval and review date on every document; review at least yearly.
Policies are read and accepted by staff, and reinforced by awareness.
Exceptions: requested, risk-assessed, accepted for a limited time with compensating controls, recorded.
PSSI: the French name for the information security policy.

example.code:
Exception register (extract)
ID     System          Rule not met        Reason                    Compensating control          Accepted by    Until
EX-07  Old ERP         MFA for admins      Not supported by version  Admin access only from 2 PCs  CFO            31 Mar
EX-09  Print supplier  Right to audit      Supplier refused clause   SOC 2 type II report yearly   Purchasing dir 30 Jun
example.note: Each exception has an owner who accepts the risk, a compensating control and an end date.

lessons.title: Access management: the control auditors always test
text: Identity and access management decides who can do what in which system. It is tested in almost every audit because excessive or forgotten access is behind many incidents and frauds. Its principles are least privilege (each person has only the access needed for the job), need to know, and segregation of duties: no single person should be able to carry out a sensitive process alone, for example create a supplier and approve its payment.

Access follows the joiner-mover-leaver process. Joiner: access is requested by the manager, approved, granted according to a role profile, and recorded. Mover: when someone changes job, new access is granted and the old one is removed; forgetting this step is how people accumulate rights over the years. Leaver: all access is removed on the last day, ideally automatically from the HR system, including SaaS tools and shared accounts.

Privileged accounts, such as system administrators and database owners, need stronger controls: named accounts rather than shared ones, MFA, a separate account from the everyday one, logging of what they do, and a vault for the few shared technical passwords. Service accounts used by applications must have an owner and no interactive login.

The access review is the main detective control. Periodically (often quarterly for sensitive systems, yearly for others), the system owner receives the list of users and their rights, confirms or removes each one, and the removals are done and checked. A good review is complete (the list comes straight from the system), dated, signed, and its removals are traced to tickets. A review where the manager answers “all OK” in two minutes for 400 users is a classic audit finding.

When you test access, compare three lists: the HR list of employees and leavers, the accounts in the system, and the approvals. Accounts of people who left, accounts with no owner and rights that do not match the job are the most frequent findings. You can do this comparison with a spreadsheet or a few SQL queries.
points: Least privilege, need to know, segregation of duties.
Joiner-mover-leaver: approve and record, remove old rights on a move, remove everything on the last day.
Privileged accounts: named, MFA, separate from daily use, logged.
Access review: complete list from the system, decision per user, removals executed and traced.
Test by comparing HR leavers, system accounts and approvals.

example.code:
Access test, finance system, 30 June
HR leavers since 1 January ............ 18
Of which still with an active account .. 3   -> finding: leaver process not applied
Accounts with no matching employee ..... 2   -> 1 service account without owner, 1 old trainee
Users who can create AND pay suppliers . 4   -> segregation of duties conflict
Access requests without approval (25 sampled) .. 1
example.note: Typical results of an access test; each line becomes a finding with an owner and a corrective action.

lessons.title: Measuring and reporting to management
text: Governance needs information. Management cannot read a 300-line risk register, so the GRC team turns it into a few indicators and a clear story. Key performance indicators show whether security processes work: the percentage of staff who completed awareness training, the share of critical patches applied within the target time, the number of overdue audit actions. Key risk indicators warn that a risk is growing: phishing click rate rising, more accounts without MFA, more suppliers without a security review.

A good indicator has a definition, a source, an owner, a frequency and thresholds: green, amber and red, agreed in advance. It must be produced the same way each time, ideally from systems rather than from manual counting. Too many indicators hide the important ones: a security committee usually follows ten to fifteen.

The risk appetite statement, approved by management, says how much risk the organisation accepts in each area, for example “no critical system without a tested backup” or “no high residual risk without an action plan”. Indicators are compared with it: an indicator in the red means a decision is needed, not only information.

A monthly or quarterly report usually contains the top risks and how they moved, the indicators against their thresholds, the status of audit and action plans with overdue items named, incidents of the period and lessons learned, new regulations and their impact, and the decisions requested. Write it for busy readers: one page of summary first, the detail in an appendix.

GRC tools such as ServiceNow GRC, Archer, OneTrust or, in start-ups, Vanta and Drata, hold the registers, the controls, the evidence and the workflows, and produce the dashboards. Many organisations still start with spreadsheets and a dashboard in Power BI; the method matters more than the tool.
points: KPI: is the process working? KRI: is the risk growing?
Each indicator: definition, source, owner, frequency, green/amber/red thresholds.
Risk appetite statement approved by management; red indicators call for a decision.
Report: top risks, indicators, overdue actions, incidents, regulation, decisions needed.
Tools help (ServiceNow GRC, Archer, OneTrust, Vanta, Drata), but method comes first.

example.code:
Security committee, Q3            Value   Target   Status
Staff trained this year            91%    >= 95%   amber
Critical patches within 14 days    78%    >= 90%   red    -> decision: extra team for 6 weeks
Phishing test click rate            6%    <= 8%    green
Admin accounts with MFA           100%    100%     green
Audit actions overdue                 5    0        red    -> owners named, new dates
Suppliers reviewed (critical)      14/16   16/16   amber
example.note: A one-page indicator table: the red lines come with the decision requested from the committee.

items: Direction, roles, rules and risk appetite set by management
Identify, assess, treat and monitor risks
Meet laws, standards and contracts, and prove it
1: business owns and runs controls; 2: risk and compliance frame and challenge; 3: internal audit assures
Anything of value: information, systems, people, sites, suppliers

pitfalls: Writing policies nobody reads: a policy is only a control when people know it and it is applied.
Treating compliance as the goal: a certificate does not prove that the main risks are under control.
Asking IT to own every risk: assets and risks belong to business owners, IT runs many of the controls.
Collecting evidence the week before the audit: build it into the process so it exists all year.
Running one project per standard instead of one control set mapped to all of them.
Accepting “all OK” access reviews without checking that the list was complete and the removals were done.
Reporting 40 indicators: management needs a few, with thresholds and the decisions required.

exercises.q: Sort these activities into governance, risk management or compliance.

groups.name: Governance
items: Management approves the information security policy
Defining who owns each information asset

groups.name: Risk management
items: Scoring the likelihood and impact of ransomware
Choosing to reduce a risk with a new control
Updating the risk register after a new project

groups.name: Compliance
items: Collecting evidence for the ISO 27001 audit
Checking a GDPR processing is in the record

exercises.answer: Governance decides direction, roles and rules; risk management assesses and treats risks; compliance checks obligations are met and proves it. In practice the three feed each other: the risk appetite (governance) tells risk management which risks must be treated, and compliance produces the evidence that the chosen controls work.

groups.name: Preventive
items: Manager approval before access is granted

groups.name: Detective
items: Alert on logins from an unusual country

exercises.answer: Preventive controls stop the event, detective controls find it after it happened or while it happens, and corrective controls limit the damage and restore normal operation. A good set of controls for a risk combines the three (defence in depth).

exercises.q: Match each term with its definition.
pairs: Something of value to protect, with a business owner
A weakness that can be exploited
A measure that reduces a risk
A dated record proving a control ran
exercises.answer: A risk exists when a threat can exploit a vulnerability on an asset; controls reduce the likelihood or the impact, and evidence proves to auditors that the controls work.

exercises.q: Match each framework or law with what it covers.
pairs: A certifiable information security management system
Six functions from Govern to Recover
An auditor’s report on a provider’s controls over a period
ICT resilience of banks, insurers and their IT providers
Cybersecurity of essential and important entities in the EU
exercises.answer: Frameworks (ISO 27001, NIST CSF, SOC 2, PCI DSS) are sets of good practices or audit criteria; NIS2 and DORA are European legal obligations. A GRC team maps one control set to all the texts that apply to it.

exercises.q: Which of these is a person in the second line?
options: The IT administrator who grants access
The CISO who sets the security framework and challenges IT
The internal auditor who tests the access process
The sales director who owns the customer database
exercises.answer: The second line sets the framework and challenges the first line: the CISO, the risk and compliance teams, the data protection officer. The administrator and the sales director are first line (they run controls or own risks), and internal audit is the third line.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a leaver process in the right order.
steps: HR records the departure date in the HR system
The HR system sends the leaver event to IT
All accounts are disabled at the end of the last day
Shared passwords the person knew are changed
The manager confirms the removal and the ticket is closed
The quarterly access review checks no leaver account remains
exercises.answer: The process starts from HR, the source of truth, removes access on the last day, deals with shared secrets, is recorded, and the access review later detects anything that was missed: a preventive process backed by a detective control.

exercises.q: During an access test you compare the HR list with the finance system. 18 people left this year, and 3 of them still have an active account. Walk through what you do.

choices.label: Ask IT to disable the 3 accounts now and check if they were used after the departure date
choices.feedback: Right: contain the risk first, then find out whether it was exploited, using the login logs.

choices.label: Write the finding in the audit report and wait for the next review
choices.feedback: The accounts stay open in the meantime: an active leaver account is a live risk, so containment comes first.

choices.label: Delete the 3 accounts and their history
choices.feedback: Deleting history destroys the evidence you need to check whether the accounts were misused. Disable, do not delete.

steps.text: The logs show no login after the departures. What is the finding?

choices.label: The leaver control did not operate effectively: 3 of 18 leavers kept access
choices.feedback: Yes: no misuse happened, but the control failed 3 times out of 18, which is an operating effectiveness finding.

choices.label: No finding, since nobody used the accounts
choices.feedback: The absence of misuse is luck, not a control. The process failed and must be fixed.

choices.label: A design finding on the password policy
choices.feedback: Passwords are not the issue here: the leaver process did not remove access.

steps.text: Which corrective action is the strongest?

choices.label: Automate account disabling from the HR system, and keep the quarterly review
choices.feedback: Right: an automated preventive control is more reliable, and the review stays as the detective layer.

choices.label: Send a reminder e-mail to all managers
choices.feedback: Reminders help a little, but the process still depends on people remembering.

choices.label: Make the access review monthly instead of quarterly
choices.feedback: It detects faster but does not prevent the problem; fix the root cause first.

exercises.answer: Contain the risk (disable, not delete), check the logs for misuse, record an operating effectiveness finding with its root cause, and fix it with an automated preventive control while keeping the detective review.

exercises.q: A fraudster changes a supplier’s bank details in the payment system. Which property of the CIA triad is attacked? One word.
exercises.answer: Integrity: the information is no longer accurate, although nothing leaked and the system stayed available. The usual controls are a second person approving any change of bank details, a call-back to the supplier on a known number, and a log of changes reviewed regularly.

exercises.q: In B6, compute the share of critical patches applied within the 14-day target, as a decimal (0.78 for 78 %).
exercises.explain: 94 / 120 = 0.78, so 78 % of critical patches met the target. With a target of 90 % the indicator is red, and the 8 patches not applied yet are the first thing to explain to the committee.

exercises.q: Rewrite this control so that an auditor can test it: “Access rights are reviewed regularly.”
exercises.hint: Who, what, which system, how often, what record.
exercises.answer: Each quarter, the owner of the finance system receives from IT the full list of accounts and roles extracted from the system on the first working day of the quarter, confirms or requests the removal of each account within 15 days, and signs the review in the ticket tool; IT removes the rights listed within 5 days and attaches the confirmation to the same ticket. This states the owner, the scope, the frequency, the source of the list, the deadline and the evidence an auditor will sample.

exercises.q: A business manager asks for an exception: a legacy production system cannot use multi-factor authentication. What do you do?
exercises.hint: Assess, compensate, accept, record, end date.
exercises.answer: I ask for the details: which system, which accounts, why MFA is impossible and when the system will be replaced. I assess the risk with IT: who can reach the system, from where, and what an attacker could do. I propose compensating controls, for example access only from two administration workstations through a VPN with MFA, named accounts, strong passwords and logging with alerts. The risk owner, a senior business manager, formally accepts the residual risk for a limited period, for example until the replacement date, and I record the exception in the register with a review date. If the risk is above the appetite, the decision goes to the security committee.

exercises.q: Your manager asks for a one-page security report for the executive committee. What do you put in it?
exercises.answer: A short summary first: overall status and the two or three messages that matter. Then the top five risks with their trend since the last report and the actions under way, a small table of key indicators against their green, amber and red thresholds, the audit and action plan status naming the overdue items and their owners, notable incidents with lessons learned, upcoming regulatory changes such as NIS2 obligations, and the decisions or budget requested. Details go to an appendix. Every red item comes with a proposed decision, because executives need choices, not only information.

interview.q: What is the difference between governance, risk management and compliance?
interview.a: Governance is how management sets direction for security: roles, rules, risk appetite and oversight. Risk management finds what could go wrong, measures it and decides how to treat it. Compliance makes sure the organisation meets its obligations, from GDPR and NIS2 to ISO 27001 and client contracts, and proves it with evidence. They feed each other: governance sets the appetite that tells risk management what must be treated, and compliance checks that the chosen controls work.

The first line is the business and IT teams that own the risks and run the controls day to day. The second line, such as the CISO, risk management and compliance, sets the framework, advises and challenges the first line. The third line is internal audit, which gives the board independent assurance that the first two lines work. As a GRC analyst in the second line, I help the first line own its risks rather than doing their controls for them.

interview.q: How do you know a control works?
interview.a: I test its design and its operating effectiveness. Design: if it works as described, does it address the risk, for example does the access review cover rights and not only names? Operating effectiveness: did it run every time over the period? I take a sample, such as 25 access requests out of 300, and check the evidence: the approval, its date, who approved. Automated controls can often be tested once with their configuration plus a check that it did not change.

interview.q: What is the CIA triad? Give an example where integrity matters most.
interview.a: Confidentiality, integrity and availability are the three properties security protects. Integrity matters most for supplier bank details: if a fraudster changes them, payments go to the wrong account even though nothing was leaked and the system stayed available. Controls follow: a second person approves any change, the supplier is called back on a known number, and changes are logged and reviewed.

interview.q: How would you organise compliance with ISO 27001, SOC 2 and NIS2 at the same time?
interview.a: With one control set mapped to all three, not three projects. I build or reuse a control library, map each control to the requirements it answers, assign one owner per control and collect the evidence once in a shared place. Each audit then picks from the same evidence. Gaps specific to one text, such as NIS2 incident reporting deadlines, are added as extra controls. This reduces the work for IT and gives management one consistent view.

interview.q: What are the most common findings in an access management audit?
interview.a: Accounts of people who left that are still active, generic or shared accounts with no owner, users who kept old rights after changing jobs, segregation of duties conflicts such as creating and paying suppliers, privileged accounts without MFA, and access reviews that were approved without real checks or whose removals were never carried out. I find them by comparing the HR list, the system accounts and the approvals.

interview.q: What is the difference between a KPI and a KRI in security?
interview.a: A key performance indicator measures whether a security process works, for example the share of critical patches applied in 14 days. A key risk indicator warns that a risk is increasing, for example a rising phishing click rate or more internet-facing systems without MFA. Both need a clear definition, a source, an owner and thresholds agreed in advance, so that a red value triggers a decision.
